extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical ethics / philosophy (e.g., readers of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotle's criteria and distinctions for Justice, Equity, Voluntariness, and Intellectual Virtues (Knowledge, Art, Practical Wisdom) as parts of moral evaluation. The text lays out definitions, conditions, examples, and borderline cases used to judge actions and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as proportionate; Injustice as excess or defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is defined in terms of proportion: the Unjust is 'excess or defect of what is good or hurtful respectively, in violation of the proportionate.' Injustice aims at producing excess and defect (giving larger share of abstract good or smaller share of abstract evil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish just and unjust distributions or actions by reference to proportionality (who gets too much or too little). Examples and contrasts with self-harm and with acts toward others are given to show how proportion governs evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between unjust act and unjust character
rubrics_metrics.description: A single unjust act (e.g., stealing, adultery) does not necessarily make one an unjust person; culpability depends on whether the act was done by deliberate choice or from impulse/passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one may commit adultery from passion (acts unjustly) yet not have formed an unjust character; repeated deliberate choice is what confirms a person's character as unjust. The criterion emphasizes voluntariness and deliberation for moral character formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Justice requires mutually acknowledged law, equality, and reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Social Just arises among those who live in communion aiming at independence and equal standing; 'Just implies mutually acknowledged law, and law the possibility of injustice,' so social justice presupposes law and reciprocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies only among persons capable of reciprocal legal relations (rulers and ruled, equals). Domestic relations (master/father) instantiate different forms of justice because equality and legal reciprocity are absent or modified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural versus Conventional (Enacted) Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some justs are natural (have same force everywhere and do not depend on reception), others are conventional/enacted (depend on human decree or custom, e.g., fixed ransom price, specific sacrifices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes universal moral claims from legally/culturally contingent rules; shows how apparent variability of laws does not imply absence of natural justice. Use this to evaluate whether a rule reflects a deeper natural justice or mere convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness as condition for moral responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An act is voluntary when it is within a man's power and done with knowledge (of whom one strikes, by what instrument, and with what likely result) and not due to compulsion; involuntary acts occur through ignorance or compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed tests: if another seizes one's hand and strikes, the owner of the hand did not act voluntarily; ignorance about the person/instrument/result can render an action involuntary. This criterion governs moral blameworthiness and whether an act counts as just/unjust action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake vs Misadventure distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: When harm arises contrary to reasonable expectation and external to the agent it is a Misadventure; when the origination of the cause rests with the agent (though attended with ignorance) it is a Mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to parse culpability for unintended harms: misadventures are less attributable to the agent than mistakes, which originate in the agent even if done in ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unjust acts from passion without deliberation vs deliberate injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done with knowledge but without previous deliberation (e.g., from anger or passion) are unjust actions, but they do not necessarily render the agent a confirmed unjust person; deliberate choice is what makes the doer a confirmed unjust and depraved person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes momentary loss of control (excusable to some extent) from chosen, premeditated injustice. Evaluations should consider whether passion was 'natural' or disproportionate/unfairly attributable to weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being unjustly dealt with requires opposition to the sufferer's wish
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'unjustly dealt with' is not merely to suffer what is in itself unjust; it must be against the wish of the sufferer. One cannot be unjustly dealt with with one's own consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to cases like voluntary gift (not unjust) versus coerced taking. Use this to assess victim status: consent negates the status of being unjustly treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility in distributive injustice lies with the distributor
rubrics_metrics.description: When a wrongful allocation gives a larger share to one party contrary to the proper rate, it is the distributor who acts unjustly, not the recipient who merely receives more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies blame: even if the receiver benefits, moral agency and voluntariness of the distributor are primary. Ignorant wrongful awards mitigate responsibility; knowing wrongful adjudication demonstrates distributive injustice and motives (favor or revenge) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity (the Equitable) corrects law's universality where it is defective
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity is 'a correction of Law, where Law is defective by reason of its universality.' The Equitable is Just and often better than the letter of law in particular exceptional cases that the universal law did not foresee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equity to adapt universal legal rules to particular cases the law's generality misdescribes. The equitable person waives strict legal claims to achieve fairer outcomes; equity is praised as a moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice requires plurality; one cannot be unjust solely to oneself (in the social sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice (as a social wrong) involves plurality of persons; a man cannot in the social sense deal unjustly only to himself. Suicide or self-harm can be unjust toward the community (violating Right Reason/law), but many crimes cannot be committed against oneself (you cannot steal your own property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to delimit the scope of injustice: social/political dimensions require others; internal conflicts or self-harm are treated differently (may implicate community norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtue requires right inward dispositions, not merely outward acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing the outward acts associated with a virtue (e.g., resisting, medicating) is not sufficient; moral virtue requires doing them with particular inward dispositions and in certain ways — analogous to knowing how to administer medicine, not merely using a knife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of virtue should look beyond compliance with behavioral rules to the agent's dispositions and the manner/timing/context of actions. The analogy to medicine stresses skillful, context-sensitive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mean as defined by Right Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral excellence is choosing the mean between excess and defect 'according to the dictates of Right Reason.' The mean is relative and must be specified by Right Reason rather than mere formulaic admonitions to 'moderation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques simplistic guidance; one must define what 'Right Reason' requires in each domain. Practical prescriptions (like a physician's guidance for when/how to apply remedies) are needed for actionable moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the soul and functions relevant to moral evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul contains Rational and Irrational parts; the Rational divides into that which knows (necessary things) and the Calculative (deliberative) part. Moral choice arises when intellect and will (appetition) interact rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these psychological-functional distinctions to evaluate responsibility and virtue: moral choice requires both correct intellectual operation and rightly directed will (appetition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual excellences: Art, Knowledge, Practical Wisdom, Science, Intuition (definitions and roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle lists five intellectual excellences (Art, Knowledge, Practical Wisdom, Science, Intuition). Knowledge concerns necessary/eternal truths and is teachable and demonstrative (syllogistic); Art is 'a state of mind, conjoined with true Reason, apt to Make' (production); Practical Wisdom is the capacity to deliberate well about living well and to calculate for good ends where there is no definite rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions to distinguish types of intellectual competence relevant to moral action: Knowledge for theoretical truth; Art for productive skill; Practical Wisdom for deliberation about ends in contingent human life. The text emphasizes teachability, sources (induction/syllogism), and relation to deliberation.
